newsitem.title: CHILE: Chileans seen voting for continuity in Sunday poll.
newsitem.headline: Chileans seen voting for continuity in Sunday poll.

text.p: Chileans, enjoying a Latin American rarity of a growing economy and stable government, are expected to give President Eduardo Frei's ruling coalition a strong victory in nationwide municipal elections on Sunday.
Opinion polls suggest Frei's Christian Democratic Party will win a sizeable plurality of between 25 and 30 percent of the vote, in a field of nine parties.

But two left-wing partners in the coalition, the Party for Democracy (PPD) and the Socialists, are expected to make gains and strengthen the left's hand in the coalition before presidential elections in 1999, analysts said.
"The country's fate is not hanging on these elections, but they will have an impact on the next elections," said Marta Lagos, a political scientist and pollster.

Strong showings by the PPD and the Socialists will almost certainly put the popular Public Works Minister Ricardo Lagos, a PPD man and well-known opponent of military rule in the 1980s, in a better position to become the coalition candidate for president in 1999, she said.
Polls show Lagos is the only politician in Chile more popular than Frei.

But the country's best-known mayor, Santiago's Jaime Ravinet, a Christian Democrat, is expected to win reelection easily and could use a victory to nurture his own presidential ambitions, analysts said.

"Of the mayors seeking reelection, I think the vast majority are going to win," said Ravinet, known for his dapper suits, bright red hair and his campaigns to clear street hawkers and pushcarts off city sidewalks.

Frei, who took office in 1994 as Chile's second elected leader after the end of military rule in 1990, has succeeded in holding together the often fractious coalition known as "La Concertacion" through political crises and rivalries.
He has been helped by prosperity -- Chile has had 14 years of uninterrupted economic growth, a feat unmatched in Latin America -- and a general feeling of stability in government.

But polls show Chileans are growing impatient to feel more the benefits of growth, a trend that could help the far-left Communists. Marta Lagos said the Communists could raise their number of mayoral seats from one to half a dozen.

Two right-wing parties are expected to win roughly the same combined vote they won in municipal polls in 1992, about 25 percent, with their support concentrated in Santiago's wealthier suburbs and the south.
The four parties in the Concertacion are expected to win a combined 50 to 60 percent, with the rest divided between smaller parties and independents.

The elections will mark the first time Chileans will pass judgment on Frei's government at the polls since he took office, and will point to trends before parliamentary elections next year, analysts said.
"Chilean elections in general have their peculiar characteristics but they always give a sign of what's going to happen in the future," said Juan Seron, an analyst at the University of Chile.
